utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Inger de Ru, Rafael La Cruz, and Barney Thomas for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to all. Colin Morrison, Chad Mair, Boris Zorko, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with the Court's indulgence, we will call our next witness, Mr. Ivan Djokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djokic. You may take a seat, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, we have prepared a binder for Mr. Djokic which I think he'll be needing in short order. So if he could be given the opportunity to have that by his side, I think it might be of assistance in the efficiency of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just before you begin, Mr. Guy-Smith, I don't know whether your colleagues on the opposite side might have this document, but I didn't find it in the witness's report, I don't have his curriculum vitae, so I'm not quite --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure how he qualifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll take care of that in quite short order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djokic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when you were born, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 27th of October, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I was born in Stanisinci village Vrnjacka Banja municipality in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please wait for the end of the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters say could you wait for the end of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I actually didn't hear anything from the interpreter at all, so there might be something wrong with my system. If we could just double-check with them quickly. I mean, I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel hear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hello?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now I can hear, yes. Thank you. And I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you currently employed, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I work at the state university of Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in what capacity do you work at the state university in Novi Pazar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I'm a lecturer at the university, teaching four courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what courses are you teaching?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The basics of information and technology, information -- computer networks, computer network protocols, and computer network security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is that a course for civilians, for military, is it a mixed course? What kind of students are you teaching?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: It's a civilian university and these are postgraduate students from years 1 through 4 of a -- rather, undergraduate students from years 1 through 4 of the state university.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could please have up on the screen 65 ter 07001D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I refer you to -- sir, I refer you to tab B in the binder. It hasn't come up yet. While we're waiting for the document to come up, did you have occasion during your professional career to be employed in the military?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a lieutenant-general, a retired lieutenant-general, and I practically spent my entire professional career in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see that the document has now come up on the screen, and I would like you to take a look at this, if you could. I believe this is your curriculum vitae that you presented in relationship to the work that you've done in this case. If we could focus on the fourth entry in this document, it says between 1970 and 1973 you were at the aeronautical military academy in Rajlovac, Yugoslavia. What were your duties there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Once I completed my secondary schooling, I got enrolled in the military academy, and this was the first schooling that I had at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And starting at the bottom of the page, moving to the top of the page, in between 1978 and 1990 what were you doing, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Once I graduated from the academy in Rajlovac, and that was between 1970 and 1973, I graduated from a higher level aeronautical academy in Belgrade. And then from 1978 onwards, I worked for the aeronautical institute in Zarkovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after you worked for the aeronautical institute in Zarkovo, what were your next duties with regard to the military, if you could tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: My next duty was also with then the aeronautical profession, and I worked as the head of the aeronautical administration within the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to that work, when you say that you worked within the Main Staff, what part of the Main Staff did you work with? Did you work in any particular department at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Between 1994 and 2000, I was the head of the aeronautical administration, and that's the title of this particular body which is charged with the overall maintenance of air force and anti -- or rather, anti-aircraft defence assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your work in that area, were you tasked with dealing with issues concerning logistics?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The maintenance of assets is one aspect of logistics, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the years 2000 and 2001, could you tell us what your specific duties and tasks were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In 2000 and 2001, I worked as the head of the operational and logistics administration which could be said to be the operational part of the logistics in the General Staff and charged with providing precisely that, operational logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "operational logistics," could you please explain to the Chamber what you mean by that particular term, "operational logistics"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: What I mean by operational or operative logistics is long-term and short-term planning of all segments of logistics. It is in that area that all the elements come together which constitute the logistic support of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what are those elements that constitute logistic support of an army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In the report that I submitted, you will have seen that logistical support of the VJ, and previously JNA, was termed rear support, or support for the rear. Which basically means the same thing, it's just a different way of going about it. Elements of that support for the rear include technical support, aeronautical support, naval maintenance support, quartermaster support which includes the provision of food and clothing for troops, then traffic support or transport support, medical support, et cetera. All these are elements of logistics under the rules of the support provided for the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your duties between 2001 and 2003, what were you tasked to do?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: My duties were to co-ordinate the plans of logistic support services to make sure that these plans are consistently applied and to see to it that all these plans are properly implemented in the various logistic support services.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And between 2003 and 2004 what were your duties, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Between 2003 and 2004, I was at a higher step within the chain of logistic support and I was assistant Chief of the Main Staff for logistics, of the General Staff, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then in 2004 and 2005, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In 2004 and 2005, I worked within the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and Montenegro since I had been transferred to the ministry as an officer to the post of assistant minister for materiel resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your knowledge and experience in the area of logistics, have you been involved in any projects that have as a component part logistics issues?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Well, practically my entire professional career has been spent in the area of logistics and logistical support starting from the aeronautical institute where I worked in the research for the development of the related technology, so that's to say logistical technology. All the subsequent duties that I had within the General Staff also fell within the field of logistics which we call consumer logistics; in other words, all the various issues that are there to make sure that the troops can work properly. As the chief of the aeronautical administration, I also worked in the field of maintenance and repair of various assets and to -- and I also worked in the field of developing new ways of approaching maintenance and service of these assets since technology in this field is constantly updated and upgraded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move Mr. Djokic's CV for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D505. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 4001D on the screen. 04001D. And before I go any further, to refresh all of our recollection, in a filing by the Prosecution on the 16th of July, 2010, the Prosecution indicated that it challenged neither the qualification nor the relevance of the report of Mr. Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before you is a document which is a -- entitled "Yugoslav Army Logistical Support 1992-1998 Expert Report." Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I produced the document for the purposes of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the document is both up on the screen as well as I've supplied with you a clean, hard copy of the document in your binder which is the first copy in the binder. You are free to use either one which is easier for your use.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Guy-Smith kindly either speak up or speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I heard you and I will do both.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've given us a brief introduction with regard to the topic of logistics, and in your brief remarks you use the term "rear support" at one point. And I'm wondering if could you expand on this term or explain the particular significance of that term within the military that you worked?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army and in the early days of the Army of Yugoslavia, troops received support through rear support, which is synonymous with logistical support. However, the organisation and efficiency of rear support is not on the same plane with that of logistical support. For this reason, in a later period, the Army of Yugoslavia re-organised rear support in order to move on to a more efficient concept of logistical support. What is the crucial difference between the two? The rear support is under the command of a commander who has his assistant for rear support. An assistant may propose and carry out commanders' decisions. Under logistical support, you have a logistics commander whose powers are far broader. He may plan, decide, and carry out his decisions. This would be the essential difference. Now, the purpose of both the rear support and logistical support is one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What is that purpose, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The purpose of logistical support is to enable army units to carry out their tasks and to create conditions for the army's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't want to go through your report with you verbatim, but what I would like to do is just identify a couple of things, if I could. And since we have been talking about logistical support and rear support, I take it that is the topic that is discussed in chapter 2 of the report that you've submitted; correct? And I think it might be of assistance just to take a look at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned in a discussion that we've just had, you mentioned the Yugoslav People's Army and the Army of Yugoslavia. Are those two different armies?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: These are two different armies because when the Yugoslav People's Army ceased to exist, the Army of Yugoslavia was set up. The Yugoslav People's Army was the armed force of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whereas the Army of Yugoslavia is the armed force of -- or was the armed force of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of logistical support, were the functions of the head of the army different under the Yugoslav People's Army and under the Army of Yugoslavia or were they the same?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The concept of rear support was taken over from the Yugoslav People's Army, thus the Army of Yugoslavia also used the concept of rear support rather than logistical support. It was only at a later date that the Army of Yugoslavia introduced certain novelties in the powers of commanders, in the powers of the Ministry of Defence, and the powers of the General Staff. At that point, through a long-lasting transformation process, the concept of rear support was abandoned in favour of logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this has nothing to do with you for the moment. I may have been not speaking into the microphone, I may have misspoke, or I may have spoken too softly, but with regards to the word on line 2 of page 10, I asked the question of "with regard to the issue of logistical" - not "local" - support. The word should be "logistical." Just so that the record is clear in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a shift or a transformation from one army to the other, and I'd like to for a moment focus on one of the statements that you've made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have paragraph 52, which would be in the B/C/S page 18 and in the English page 20, up on the screen, I would be most appreciative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus on in paragraph 20 -- in paragraph 52 you were discussing the Federal Ministry of Defence in the VJ General Staff, and you indicate here that the legal regulations - I'm about halfway through that paragraph: "The legal regulations were such that the overall management of the army in ensuing conditions for its development and functioning (which includes logistical support of the army) was completely entrusted to the civilian and parliamentary authorities." I'd like to see if you could expand on that and explain to the Chamber perhaps a bit more fully what you mean by that and the following sentences.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In any army there is a degree of overlap between the General Staff or the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence with respect to logistical support. The issue is who would be the one disposing of the assets reserved for the military and who would have the main say. It was especially pronounced during periods of army transformation. Sometimes the power of decision lay with the ministry, and at other times it was with the General Staff. In 1992, after the formation of the FRY, the entire competence pertaining to logistical acquisition, including any purchase for the needs of the army, as well as development, was handed over in its entirety to the Ministry of Defence. And they were the owner of all of the assets at the disposal of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what is the significance of the Ministry of Defence being in the position to be the owner of all of the assets?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The importance of it is that the minister of defence, when proposing budgets, is the enforcing agent in terms of that budget vis-à-vis the Assembly. He has the main say on what the annual army budget is going to look like. Once adopted, he is the one supervising the implementation of the budget. He is the one who has a service at his disposal charged with army procurement. Once equipment is procured, it is then delivered to the army for use, and this is where the competence of the General Staff and its units begin with respect to the use of the equipment put at their disposal. Having in mind that formerly the federal secretariat for national defence which was a sort of Ministry of Defence was a solely military organisation, and as of 1992, as of the formation of the FRY, the minister of defence is a civilian. And here we can see the shift towards civilian control over army logistical matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please turn off his microphone when not putting questions. We have a lot of background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could now turn to paragraph 56 in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which will be B/C/S pages 19 and 20 and English pages 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you discuss the characteristics or logistics in warfare and specifically discuss issues with regard to the dissolution of the SFRY and development in issues that abounded logistics, and I would like to refer you to and pay attention to section A, which will be on the next page in both. And specifically to the statement that you make in about the middle of that section in which you say: "However, the newly formed ministries of defence in the former Yugoslavia had no precise requirements from the armed forces, no overall insight into the status of national resources, no current database, and no developed military co-operation with other countries." I'm wondering if you could explain that particular assertion more fully.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: You see, the logistical needs of an armed force is planned based on its staffing and manning levels, based on the type of organisation, and based on the tasks put before that armed force. In order to plan properly for the needs of the army within a year, that is, a short-term plan, and this is particularly important if you plan long-range, such as four-year plans, you need to have all that data at your disposal. During the break-up of Yugoslavia, new states were being created which had not had formed their armed forces yet. Their organisation was unknown, their manning levels were unknown, nor were the primary tasks of such armies known. Next, the newly formed ministries lacked information from the previous period on how the reserves were distributed, where they were stockpiled, and what their current status was. All of the initial parameters needed for short- and long-term planning were not in the hands of those ministries. That is why the ministries instead of using specific data had to make assumptions on the size of the army and its tasks. It is very difficult to plan in such situations and frequently results in improvisation and of course mistakes being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to paragraph C which is entitled "dispersed military industry," you state: "With the dissolution of Yugoslavia, a unified system of military industry became dispersed, preventing the manufacture of more complex weapons systems ..." and then you continue. Could you tell the Chamber what was the dispersal, as you put it, of the military industry upon the break-up. What was the situation prior to the break-up and what was the situation after the break-up with regard to the issue of the unified military industry or dispersed military industry?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The military industry of the SFRY, that is to say, the Yugoslavia before the break-up, for the country of that size was a successful one, one could say. It met up to 80 per cent of the needs of the army in terms of equipment and weapons systems. If one looks at the distribution of locations of the military industry, we could see that it was largely grouped towards the centre of the country in geographical terms. It was ding dated by political agendas and decisions, and it was also -- having in mind the fact that it was more easy, it was easier to defend the country from the centre than it was to put up defence lines right at the borders. It was interlinked in a way that a factory produced, say, the final product, whereas it did not produce all of the components. Those components were produced in other military or civilian factories. Perhaps I can illustrate this by way of an example. The airplanes produced in the Sokol Mostar factory, which is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the hydraulic system and steerers were produced in a factory in Trstenik, the engines were produced in a factory called Oro [phoen], the weapons systems were produced in several different locations; once Yugoslavia broke up, those factories could no longer co-operate. And never again did there come a time when an entire product could be put together. Even to date, the relations are not at such a level so as to enable the production of such a successful product as an airplane or, say, tank T-80 or M-84, which used to be produced in Croatia. We could no longer secure the components for its production. And the same went for most of such factories which produced weapons systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to take a brief digression here. And if we could have on the screen 65 ter 632D, which would be tab R, as in "rolling," in your binder. It has not yet come up on the screen in English. It has now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look at this document. You were mentioning that there were different factories in different parts of the former Yugoslavia. And looking at this particular list, could you tell us whether or not you recognise what this list represents and also where those -- let me just do that first. What this list represents.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: This table represents part of the special-purposes factories or parts of the factories which engaged in military production in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here we have the name of such factories, their locations, the type of product, the capacity of such factories, and the degree of dependence on the factories located in other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your answer, in your previous answer, with regard to where factories were, the centre of the country. Could you kindly focus us here and tell us with regard to special-purpose industrial capacities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what part of the former Republic of Yugoslavia was that? Was that the eastern part, the western part, centre part?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is the central republic of the former Yugoslavia. To my recollection, in Bosnia-Herzegovina some 45 per cent of overall production capacity was placed there in terms of military industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the break-up of the former Yugoslavia with regard to the facilities that are listed here, where or to what state or republic did those facilities become a part of and under whose control were they, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: If we look at the list, Igman and Konjic are in what now is the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bratsvo and Novi Travnik is also in Federation territory. Pretis and Vogosca is in the RS. Slavko Rodic factory in Bugojno and the Popjeda [phoen] factory in Gorazde are in Federation territory. Famos is in the RS. Soko Mostar is in the Federation. Rudi Cajavec is in the RS. That would be it, in terms of where those factories are now within the existing entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page for one remaining factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is at the bottom of your page, that's the number 10, which is the factory called Pretis Vogosca; where is that located?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Pretis is in the suburbs of Sarajevo. It is one of the larger military factories. It is now in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during the conflict was it located in the Republika Srpska or was it located in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I think that throughout the war the Pretis factory in Vogosca was under the control of Republika Srpska, although the separation line between the sides was nearby and it shifted. In any case, to the best of my recollection, I believe it was in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would seek the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, sir, can you tell me, sir, are these all the factories that were in the former Yugoslavia, or were there others in other republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is only a part of the total number of military factories. As far as I recall, for a while some 80.000 people were employed in the military industry of the former SFRY. The number of military factories is greater than you can see here. These are only those located in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If there -- the production capacity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... is there any -- may I interrupt. May I interrupt you, sir, please. Is there any reason you give us only those that are in Bosnia and Herzegovina and not those that are in the rest of the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be my error and not his, Your Honour, because in his report which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be my error, not his, Your Honour, because in his report there is a section which is directly related to the issue of distribution of military infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let him answer me, then, anyways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just don't want you to believe that the error is his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have pointed to no error whatsoever. I'm just asking, do you have any explanation, sir? Is there any reason why we are getting factories only in Bosnia and Herzegovina and not in the rest of the other republics? Or are there -- is there other table that explains, that gives us factories in the rest of the republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this expert report, I enumerated all factories involved in military production in the former Yugoslavia and I specified their locations as well as where they are, in which republics after the break-up of Yugoslavia. It is all in the report. And if needed, we can go to those parts to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D506. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving but a bit ahead for a moment, if you could go to paragraph 109 of the report, which should be, I believe it's B/C/S page 35 and English page 36. I'm sorry, it's going to be an earlier B/C/S page. It's going to be B/C/S page 34 and English page 37. Getting closer. There we go. Perfect. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Starting on this particular page and then going for the subsequent pages - and I just want to scroll through them so that His Honour is aware of that aspect of your report with regard to the question asked - could you tell us just in the broadest of senses what this part of your report entails?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In the previous part, I described the distribution of military industry and where those factories lay in terms of the newly created republics of the former Yugoslavia. The next thing I thought was important was to indicate the distribution of the infrastructure used by the military per the newly created states -- state. It is clearly shown in chapter 3.2 under the title "Distribution of Military Infrastructure." If we were to summarise the fate of military infrastructure, I could say that it remained in the locations where it had been and became part of the newly created republics. It wasn't done systematically by the army. As it was withdrawing, it was leaving behind the existing military infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in 3.21 thereafter --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- you identify the school centres and training centres throughout the region, subsequent to the dissolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You continue with that identification then you identify the military research institutes throughout the region; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: These were all school centres of the JNA which were located in these towns. I strove to show in which of the republics those school centres remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you also identified in this chapter of your report the military research institutes that existed in Slovenia, Croatia, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, Macedonia, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 3.22. Is that an accurate reflection of your report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Military research institutes are part and parcel of the logistical infrastructure of each of these countries as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You then identified throughout the area, in 3.23, the technical testing centres; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The technical testing centres within the system of logistics have the role of developing and carrying out verification testing of military equipment. This is their importance and it was for that reason that I issued them in the report. We also have the locations per towns and newly created states.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could move to the next section which is 3.24.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe, if I'm not mistaken, that in this section of your report you identify the repair and maintenance facilities throughout the region. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in section 3.25 you identify the military industry throughout the region; is that similarly correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you commented on a couple of things -- or in your earlier testimony you commented on the fact that production satisfied up to 80 per cent of the needs, if I understood your statement, with regard to the needs of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The 20 per cent that was remaining, how was that production or those needs met?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The remaining 20 per cent needs that could not be met domestically were met by purchasing on the world market. This pertains to the sophisticated, complex systems which were not manufactured in Yugoslavia. For example, the first assault-line airplanes which were purchased in the USSR, radars which were procured in Great Britain and USA. Anti-aircraft systems also purchased in Russia. These are the most blatant examples of what Yugoslavia could not manufacture in its own territory and what it had to purchase internationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you use the term "production" for the 80 per cent, who is engaged in that production? Is that the military -- what you've identified as the military industry, or is that some other sector that you are referring to in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please switch off microphone when not in use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The term "military industry factories" means only those factories whose primary production was for the military. However, one has to bear in mind that a large number of factories also produce, as a secondary manufacturing line, certain items for the military. For example, if you had a TV plant, TV and electronic plant, which mostly manufactured televisions, that plant also produced certain electronic plants for the needs of the military. So there existed not only factories which produced primarily for the military, there existed also civilian factories which had some additional manufacturing lines for the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the term "military industry" is another term that is used to identify this particular group of production the "special-purpose industry"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In the military and in Yugoslavia we use the term "special-purpose industry" because that applied to the factory which primarily produced for the military. However, in my report I use the term "military industry" because not everybody is familiar with the terms that we used back then in the former Yugoslavia and in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now I'm going to move to another subject which is: For purposes of the report that you have produced, did you attempt to have an understanding of the assets, and by that I mean the military assets, that existed throughout the former Yugoslavia before the break-up?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: My conceptual approach when it came to the distribution of assets was first of all to establish the actual assets before the break -- before the break-up. I was unable to find any document which would define precisely what assets existed in the country. This is why I used a document which I believe to be a credible one, a document which was produced for the needs of the international community. I think that OSCE engaged or commissioned an economic institute from Paris to produce this document, and all parties furnished their data to this institute, and all the data was put in the document. I believed those data to be credible. I naturally researched other documents as well, but I believed this international document to be a credible basis for my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that regard, if we could take a look at, in your report it would be paragraph 139, which -- and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe that my pagination is accurate for purposes of e-court. I believe for e-court it would be page 47 in B/C/S and page 49 in English. That's perfect. No, I was wrong; it's page 50 in English. And we need to move one page forward in B/C/S, if we could. Yes, we need to move one page forward. One page forward in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, here there is a chart, and if I'm not mistaken, the source of the information on this chart comes from the -- from CREST, Centre de Recherche en Economie et en Statistique - I hope I did that properly - as well as JNA data. So looking at this particular chart, with regard to the informations contained in this chart, is this the information that you were just referring to with regard to the weapons that were left in the former Yugoslavia before the break-up?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the data that I believed to be accurate and credible about small arms, tanks, APCs, and artillery before the break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, apart from -- apart from this particular information, if I'm understanding your report, this information is -- comes from the data source of the army; is that accurate? And by that I mean the JNA/VJ data source is one of them; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: If you look at the table we are discussing right now, I listed the data provided by the Paris institute. Then I listed the data of the JNA, which the VJ provided officially for the needs of this case. The difference between the first source and the second source of the data went from minus 0.6 and 10 per cent. And then in the following table you see -- or, rather, in the following row, you see my data, and the margin of difference is not more than 10 per cent. And after that I also listed the data by SIPRI Stockholm institute. This is the the last row in the table. And you can see that their data significantly differs from the data of the Paris institute. I believe that they made an assessment; they did not have accurate data to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you just identify for purposes of the record so we're clear, what is SIPRI?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Let me find it. It is the Stockholm institute -- I will find it in my reference materials, but I know that it is the Stockholm Peace Research Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is the information that is contained here inclusive, if you know, of the assets that were maintained by, if they were maintained by, the Territorial Defence locally in the region?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: These are total resources of the SFRY before the outbreak of the conflict. 1.621.000 pieces of small arms, 2.853 tanks, 1.775 APCs, and 6.090 pieces of artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question still stands; it has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did this include those of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as I said, these were the total resources of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, yes, total.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could go just very quickly to the very beginning of your report again, sir, I'd just like to see whether or not we can perhaps clarify aspects of your report and in the process speed up the questioning process. And all I want to do at this point is just to outline for the Chamber the areas and the chapters of your report that we have heretofore not discussed in specific and then we'll return to chapter 3. Chapter 4 discusses the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council relating to logistical support and the provision of logistical assistance to the SVK and the VRS; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Chapter 5 discusses issues concerning United Nations Security Council resolutions and attendant embargo matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Chapter 6 is an area where you engage in an analysis of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or FRY military assistance of the SVK and VRS in the period 1992 through 1995; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Chapter 7 are your final conclusions with regard to the issue of the VJ's involvement in logistical support in the period 1992 through 1998; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've had a brief discussion with Mr. Thomas, and based on that discussion as well as the previous position of the Prosecution with regard to their response to the expert report, I would at this time move the admission of the Djokic expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D507. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, if we could very briefly return to a couple of areas. If we could go back to your report, D507.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to page 83 in B/C/S and page 88 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Taking a look at the chart that is contained here, could you please describe and explain to the Chamber what you are discussing with regard to this particular chart?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: This chart shows the overview of possible weapons delivery to all warring parties in the former Yugoslavia after the embargo of the United Nations was introduced. In the first column you can see the weapons user, and in the second column you see the weapons source, where the weapons come from. The next column is the secondary assistance. And then the last column represents non-governmental participants participating in the delivery of these weapons. This is a table that I did not produce myself, rather, I took it over from a document which I considered to be credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the weapons source, focusing for the moment on the weapons user of the Bosnian Serb forces, who were the weapon sources that are identified?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this report, the forces of Bosnian Serbs received their weapons from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Israel, Russia, and Ukraine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of non-government participants, who did they receive weapons from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The non-governmental participants include various brokers which procured weapons on the legal [as interpreted] market for weapons and military equipment, and they delivered this to the forces of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you stated "various brokers procured weapons on the legal market for weapons and military equipment," could you explain what you mean by the "legal market"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I said "illegal." Illegal market of weapons means that the weapons are being procured from entities which are not authorised to distribute or sell such equipment, just as the brokers are also unauthorised to participate in this delivery of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to obtain information to determine the data to what extent or to -- or in what amounts illegal brokers were supplying weapons to the Bosnian Serb republic, and by that I mean the Republika Srpska, or to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: See, the issue of weapons delivery is so complex that anything I can say as an individual would amount to speculation. Therefore, I relied on reports of the United Nations pertaining to the embargo and the influence of the embargo on the flow of weapons. Why? Because the UN used entire teams in researching this issue. They had opportunity to talk to various governments, police officials, authorities in power. So this is why I believe their assessment to be credible. If they say that those were the possible sources for weapons delivery, then I as an individual could only speculate, and it would be pointless for me to do that. This is why I relied on reports that I believe to be credible and that I believe to be a product of a significant effort with a lot of data behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you make a determination of the change in quantities of weapons during the period of 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: We first established the initial amount of weapons held by all warring sides. There was also the UN embargo. And we also had the data about the weapons held by parties after the conflict. So it was normal to do an analysis as to the change from the beginning, how many weapons were held by the warring sides at the beginning, until the end of hostilities. And this is something that would tell us about the logistical support and the delivery of weapons during the embargo period, because we had the initial quantity of weapons and the final quantity of weapons. The initial quantities of weapons were also established in a relevant manner because all warring sides took it upon themselves in the peace agreement that they would supply the data about the weapons held by them and that they would allow for inspection of that to be carried out. Based on these reports about the quantities initially and at the end of the conflict, I made an analysis about what changes took place during the period of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would the usher are be so kind as to the move to the next page of Mr. Djokic's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I may have misinterpreted, but I wonder if the word "initial" is correct at line 20 -- sorry, page 28, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, okay, line 20. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At line 20, you say: "The initial quantities of weapons were also established in a relevant manner because all warring sides took it upon themselves in the peace agreement that they would supply the data about the weapons held by them and that they would allow for inspection of that to be carried out." And there's a question about the word "initial." Is that the word that you meant to use at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No, what I meant was final quantities, because the warring sides took it upon themselves at the end of hostilities to allow for a weapons inspection to take place. Perhaps it was a slip of the tongue or an interpretation error.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you make any determination of the quantity -- the initial quantities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... how did you go about making that determination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The initial quantities were ascertained based on the material provided by the Paris institute, as well as by the VJ and SIPRI of Stockholm. It is based on that that the initial quantities were ascertained as they existed in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the next chart, is -- could you tell us what the significance of this chart is with regard to the discussion we've just had in terms of initial quantities of weapons that were obtained from data from SIPRI, CREST, and the VJ, and the information that was obtained in the last -- the information that was obtained subsequent to the war from United Nations sources as you've identified them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I suppose we are discussing table T4?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the best way would be to illustrate this table by way of an example. In column 1 we have "type of weapon," and let's start with tanks. In column 2, under the peace agreement, the Yugoslav number of tanks was limited to 1.025. In column 3, we have the information referred to in the international community report stating that there was a surplus of tanks in excess of 1.025 which were destroyed by the FRY. The amount is 440. That in turn means that at the end of the conflict Yugoslavia had a total of 1.465 tanks. Let's go on with the "tanks" row. Croatia's number was limited to 410 under the agreement. It destroyed 3 tanks as a surplus, meaning that it had 413 tanks when the hostilities ceased. The Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a limit of 273 tanks. It destroyed 40, meaning that at the end of the conflict it had 313 tanks. And last we have Republika Srpska which, under the agreement, had the limited number of tanks of 137. It destroyed 283, meaning that Republika Srpska at the end of the conflict had 420 tanks. The same principle applies to other weapons categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to what you've just told us, I take it that if we are to look at figure number 23, since we are discussing the issue of tanks - actually it would be figures number 22 and 23 which would be on the next page for both English and B/C/S - that you have reflected in a graphic fashion, that information which we were just discussing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: That is correct. If I may, I'd like to use a couple of sentences to explain figure 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In figure 22 we can see that the FRY at the beginning of the conflict had 1.530 tanks. When the conflict ceased, it had 1.465 tanks. The Republic of Croatia, at the beginning of the conflict at 300 tanks; at the end, 413. The Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the beginning of the conflict had 85 tanks; at the end, 313. And lastly, Republika Srpska at the beginning of the conflict had 390 tanks; and at the end, 420. Figure 23 is based on the information contained in figure 22. It states that at the time of the embargo the number of tanks in the FRY was reduced by 65. In the Republic of Croatia, it increased by 113. In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it increased by 228. And in Republika Srpska, it increased by 30 tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Now, if we were to take a look at the next page, I take it that you've engaged in the same exercise in giving a graphic description, for armoured personnel carriers in figures 24 and 25, artillery weapons in figures 26 and 27, as specific line items in your analysis; and then ultimately you have graphically produced all of the changes in figure number 28, which would be, I believe, on the next page where it says, "Change in Quantity of Weapons 1992 through 1996." Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of the change in weapons, were you able to determine the actual sources of those specific weapons that you have identified in these particular charts? And by specific sources, we understand that you have mentioned both brokers as well as a number of nation states in previous charts. But were you able to obtain information that specifically identified the delivery of any particular weapon by any particular broker or nation state during the conflict period?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I did not want to speculate on the sources of weapons, that is why I merely stated that in the media and in serious analyses as well as in the documents of certain governments there is indicia as to the way how the weapons quantities increased with the respective warring parties. An individual alone, I believe, cannot offer a credible analysis of everything that is contained in that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to move on to another issue that exists, I take it, within not only the logistics, but also within your report, and that is the issue of fuel. And were you able to determine where in your report the various parties to the conflict were obtained their fuel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The supply of oil was a critical logistical element. Not only was it critical for the warring parties, but it was also a key or a critical issue in Yugoslavia itself. It is a known fact that the general embargo that was imposed prohibited the delivery of crude oil or oil derivatives to Yugoslavia and the warring parties. What I was able to ascertain is the following: In the Army of Yugoslavia, the fuel available was dispersed; from the level of 40 per cent of planned reserves, it went down to below 20 per cent of such reserves. I know from the experience of the air force that because of the lack of fuel, the training of pilots was reduced. Out of the usual 100 flying hours a day [as interpreted], they each flew perhaps up to 10 hours every year. It all indicates the very serious issue of fuel shortage. I believe the same problem existed with the other warring parties. And they simply found ways around that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct that you said "... out of the usual 100 flying hours a day"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Annually. Pilots are trained to fly about 100 hours per year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you so much. But the thing is you were interpreted as saying "a day," and I was beginning to wonder how many hours there are in a day. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to determine where the Republika Srpska was obtaining its oil supplies and its oil derivative supplies during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In the report I referred to a source specifying the smuggling channels of oil into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Perhaps that could be of assistance to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could then go to paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is figure 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is right above paragraph 251, which I believe will be on page 95 in the B/C/S and 101 in the English. Yes, if we could go down to figure 30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at figure 31, we can see that from the west the fuel found its way to the FRY from Croatia through the territory of Republika Srpska Krajina, which is marked as 1, as well as from Croatia through Republika Srpska, which is number 2, via Banja Luka, and then on to Belgrade. We can hence draw a conclusion that parts of -- certain quantities of that fuel that was supposed to go to Yugoslavia remained in Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. I believe I came across a document when compiling this report which stated that the warring sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina mutually exchanged logistical aid. For example, the Army of Republika Srpska provided artillery support and artillery ammunition to the Croatian Defence Council, and the Croatian Defence Council in turn provide the the VRS with fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 7002D on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, could you tell us what the date of this document is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the subject matter that's being discussed, could you tell us what is being discussed in this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from the document, it was pursuant to the request of the General Staff of the Serbian Army of Republika Srpska. By virtue of this order, an approval was given to provide 25.000 litres of D2 fuel and 15.000 litres of petrol to the Military Post 7088 Novi Grad from the reserves of NIK-Dvor na Uni. I believe the order is to the effect that some fuel reserves be provided from the company mentioned for the needs of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you indicated "the company mentioned," and what company would that be? Is that the company NIK-Dvor na Uni?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I presume that NIK-Dvor na Uni, although I'm not familiar with that company, was located there. I see that they had their commercial service, and I see that it was not related to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you "see that they had their commercial service," are you able to discern whether or not, from an examination of this document, this was a private contract between a private company in the VRS or the Republika Srpska, or is this some other form of transaction?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Perusing a number of document, I specified in the expert analysis that the logistical support of the VRS as well as of the other armies was not centralised and properly organised. Most of it did not go through the Main Staff, instead a lot of it was done at the local level. Here we see a request which specifies that some fuel needs to be the provided for the needs of the army at a local level. It would logically follow that there is a contract in existence, or at least there should be, specifying that this company was to sell the requested amounts of fuel to the state which would be paid for by the Ministry of Defence. That would have been the normal way to go about it. Whereas this indicates that they simply improvised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would seek its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D508. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going back to the last chart that we were looking at which identified the routes of delivery of fuel, I note that the term on that chart was "oil smuggling routes." And that's -- once again, it's on page 101 of the English and on 99 of the B/C/S. With regard to this particular chart, were you able to determine the universe of parties that were smuggling fuel inter-region, and specifically, apart from what you've mentioned here, in terms of the relationship between Croatians and the Republika Srpska, any other parties that were smuggling fuel to the Republika Srpska or to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I'd rather not go into individual assessments of who was involved, but it is clear that private individuals were involved, companies, as well as states. The smuggling of oil in large quantities is impossible without the participation of different levels, starting with private entrepreneurs, to companies, to governmental bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd now like to go to Chapter 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you are going to chapter something, can I just ask a question here, please. Sir, I see from this figure 31 that it looks like this oil that's being smuggled seems to be all destined for what is today called Serbia; am I right, looking at those arrows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was there no oil that was going to other areas? Or were you not aware of if?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the embargo was imposed on all sides, and I know that all sides had oil during the war, which means that, certainly, oil found its way into the other areas that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. But from your research to the -- inasmuch as you've researched that the oil as shown on figure 31 was going to Serbia, were you not able to find from your research how it got to other areas and where it came from? Or is there -- is there -- I don't remember seeing it when I read your report, but -- or is there another figure that shows the distribution of oil to other parts of former Yugoslavia in this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not produce a relevant document for that purpose, and I didn't want to present my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. I'm not asking for your assumptions; I'm asking for the results of your research. Inasmuch as figure 31, I suppose, is the result of your research, I'm asking: Don't you have a similar result of your research with respect to other areas? You can say, Yes, I have it, No, I don't have it. I just want to know if you have that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't come across documents similar to the one I have discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving on to chapter 6 of your report which discusses the issue of FRY military assistance to the RSK and RS, 1992 to 1995, I would first of all like to take a look at the chart that exists. It's figure number 32, which would be -- I believe it's page 106 in the English and 106 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this particular chart, could you explain to us, as a result of the research and analysis you did, what this chart graphically shows?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: This chart shows that the units of the Army of Republika Srpska received their supplies in three different ways: The first way was when the government of the Army of Republika Srpska procured materiel for the needs of the army. The materiel was supplied to the Main Staff of the VRS, and then Main Staff distributed this materiel to local units. The second way was for the Main Staff of the VRS to use the funds from the budget, or other funds, to procure materiel and to distribute it to its subordinate units. And the third way, which was the predominant one throughout the period of the conflict in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was for the units to receive their supplies locally. Which means that materiel was supplied to them by municipalities, local companies, institutions, and so on. They would procure the materiel and directly distribute it to the units locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this issue of the municipalities, local companies, and institutions procuring the materiel and distributing it, were you able to determine any percentage amount which the local municipalities and companies were responsible for in giving logistical aid and assistance to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska which was tasked by the government to provide supplies for the logistical needs of the army did an analysis about local supplies coming in from municipalities. Based on that research that they conducted, 55 per cent of municipalities which had sent in their data to the ministry provided about 70 per cent of the supplies needed by the army. Which says that the predominant way of supplying the army was done at the local level, not in a centralised way, which is contrary to the rules of logistical supplies. If we were to take into account all municipality with a margin of error of about 2 per cent, we could say that 80 per cent of the needs of the army were met at the local level, whereas the ministry and the Main Staff provided the remaining 20 per cent of the supplies needed by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss with you, if we could, the issue of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could take a look at figure, I believe it's 37 in report, which is on -- I believe it's on page 111 in English and 110 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what you are discussing here with regard to the issue of ammunition supplies in figure 37?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: This is the data from the VRS. They provide this data in their report on combat readiness. And we can consider their reports on combat readiness to be reliable, credible documents. It says here that the Army of Republika Srpska, in 1992, received 72 per cent of ammunition from materiel reserves. They received from the war booty 4 per cent, 1 per cent from the repair sources, 2 per cent from production sources, and 21 per cent from assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the percentages that you've just described to us, could you tell us - and I think you discuss this in your report in paragraph 281 which would be on the preceding page in both languages - the sources of these percentages?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The reports on combat readiness of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm asking a little bit more textured a question here for the moment which is, you said 72 per cent was received from reserves; where did those reserves come from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army had been stationed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some of the units which withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia were also transferred to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These units which were in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina had their reserves in warehouses. The Territorial Defence, which also existed there, had its own ammunition warehouses. The Yugoslav People's Army, upon its withdrawal, left part of its reserves in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The entire reserves of the Territorial Defence remained also in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, the Army of Republika Srpska took over everything that was in the territory under its control and thus created its own materiel reserves. Therefore, when we say materiel reserves, this is -- these are the reserves that come partially from the Territorial Defence and partially from the Yugoslav People's Army's reserves and partially from the reserves held by the state at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the figure of 21 per cent, could you kindly give us an explanation with regard to what does that 21 per cent -- what is that 21 per cent comprised of in terms of sources?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: This assistance was not accurately defined in the report, but I suppose that this implies local sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you also indicate that it implies military assistance from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: As for the reserves remaining after the withdrawal of the JNA and could be identified as assistance coming from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, then, yes, this would fall under this term "assistance," which represents 21 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just get clarification here. Reading in paragraph 281 of your report, you make a clear distinction between assistance and reserves. Now -- you are now saying the reserves are part of the 21 per cent. From your paragraph you said the reserves formed part of the 72 per cent, and the 21 per cent is made up of purchases by local authorities, individuals, as well as military assistance from the FRY. Am I -- am I interpreting your paragraph correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I will try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav People's Army withdrew in May. It withdrew from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The materiel belonging to the JNA that remained at that point in time went into the reserves. However, from May until the end of that year, there also came in assistance from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say, this happened after the withdrawal of the JNA, and this is part of the assistance of 21 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you say that assistance came from after May to the end of that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That clarifies. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could now turn to -- if we could now turn to table T6, which would be -- it's over -- it's going to be over one page in both languages. Page 112 in the English and 106 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In this chart here, the chart here, T6 is the chart that explains, as I believe you were referring to earlier, the estimated quantities of weapons, ammunition, and fuel that remained in the Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina after the withdrawal of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to go to the next page, page 28 -- which is paragraph 289 in which you make some conclusions with regard to the issue of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think what's going to happen, Your Honours, is you'll see there's a graph on the bottom of his page, which we don't have yet, but that will be on our next page in English. But we'll be dealing with that momentarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us the figures that are represented in 289(a), (b), and (c).

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In order to make an assessment of the amount of assistance in ammunition, I used the following approach: First of all, to establish what was the usage of ammunition by the Army of Republika Srpska, and also to use all the available documents to establish the delivery of ammunition by the Army of Yugoslavia. Based on the documents from the analysis of combat readiness of the Army of Republika Srpska, in 1994, they used 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of small arms ammunition. We don't have data from 1993 and 1995, and I assume that the usage then was the same in 1994 because there wasn't a significant change in the strength of the army. And I also used the data on what was the usage in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Apparently the interpreters did not hear the number that you had indicated. You said: "Based on the documents from the analysis of combat readiness of the Army of Republika Srpska, in 1994, they used ..." what amount?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: 2.864 tons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next page in English and remain on the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at figure 39, could you please explain to the Chamber what that chart represents?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: On this figure we see the usage of ammunition, which is defined here as the needs, 2.864 tons. And then at the bottom we see the assistance that came in from the VJ. How did I receive the data on the VJ assistance? I added up the quantities of ammunition that was mentioned in the order to provide assistance, also materiel lists on issuing assistance, materiel lists on receipt of ammunitions, as well as materiel lists on the transport of ammunition. So anything that indicated that some ammunition was given to the VRS was added up. And this is how we arrived at the quantities mentioned here. Therefore, in 1993, based on that data, they provided 232.4 tonnes. In 1994 they provided 193.8 tonnes. And in 1995 the Army of Yugoslavia provided to the VRS 42.1 tons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just to make sure in terms of what you just said because of the kinds of data that you relied upon, were you over-inclusive or under-inclusive with regard to the information that you relied upon? Did you reject any information that showed in any sense whatsoever any form of delivery to the VRS by the VJ because it may have suffered from some other impediment or concern that you have, or did you include all documents that you saw in this regard?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid any contention when it comes to quantities, I used all of the documents that indicated that something was provided by the VJ to the VRS. I even used the documents that had not been signed and that had not been stamped but did have some information about supplies. So I used them as well and added up all figures. So this is the worst-case scenario, that namely everything mentioned in the documents was indeed implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to figure number 40, what does figure number 40 reflect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's going to have to be the next page in -- thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doesn't figure number 40 reflect the same thing as figure 39 but this time with respect to artillery, as against small arms?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to -- that it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to His Honour's helpful suggestion which was contained in the question that he asked, did you come to a conclusion with regard to the scope of assistance in regards to small arms ammunition and artillery ammunition? And I'm referring you specifically to paragraph 290(a) and (b).

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
