utterances.text: If we look at the usage of ammunition in the VRS and what the Army of Yugoslavia provided in terms of assistance, when it comes to small arms weapons, the maximum of assistance was 8.11 per cent of the ammunition used for 1993, whereas for artillery ammunition, the maximum assistance amounted to 12 per cent of the ammunition used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And finally in paragraph -- I'm sorry, chapter number 7, you draw a series of conclusions, from paragraphs 333 through and including 344, with regard to the information that's contained in your report. Do you stand by those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Djokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the hour. Do you wish me to start for five minutes, or shall we break and I can recommence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to finish today?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No. I will go into tomorrow I think, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. One procedural matter, Your Honours. Exhibit P1214 has what can be described as currently an incomplete English translation. I've discussed the matter with my learned friends of the Defence who agree that this is -- this can be replaced with a complete English translation which is available. I've discussed that with the senior Legal Officer, Mr. Registrar, my learned friends don't object, and I'm seeking an order, Your Honours, to make that -- make that replace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct, and we join in Mr. Thomas's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is P1214?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: P1214, Your Honours. It's a VRS document annexing a number of tables and accounts. And what's happened is that the title to some of the tables has been translated without the table itself being reproduced, so the new version of the English simply has the table included as well as the title. At the moment, all we have on some pages is a title of the table without the table itself on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you you asking for? What is your request now?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: A replacement of the existing English translation with the one that includes the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Everything. Okay. Fine. It's so granted. May it please be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It has been replaced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: General Djokic, good afternoon. My name is Barney Thomas. I am a lawyer for the Prosecution. I have the opportunity at this stage in the proceedings of asking you questions about your testimony and about your report. I will endeavour to ask questions that are easily understandable, but please let me know if there's anything that you don't understand or anything that you are not sure about and I will rephrase my questions to you. Please, sir, listen carefully to my question and only answer the question that I'm asking and we will be able to conclude this much faster than otherwise. Is that all clear, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. General, I'd like to begin, please, with a document which you have already referred to; it is D506.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And I wonder if we could have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You will recognise this, sir, as your table of -- I'm sorry, a table of FRY special-purpose industry facilities -- I'm sorry, SFRY special-purpose industry facilities which were located on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time immediately prior to the dissolution of the SFRY. Do I understand this table correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: You do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: In the table, you have identified those republics upon which certain facilities were dependent. For example, if you look at the first entry, the Igman facility, we have a recognition there that it was dependent upon Serbia for gun powder, brass, lead, and antimony. What's -- what is antimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The factory called Igman is in Konjic in the territory of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its production programme encompasses --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, just pause. Please just listen. I apologise, it was a long question and it may have been my fault. Please listen carefully to my question. Sir, what is antimony, first of all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Antimony is a material used in the production of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Prior to the break-up, the Igman facility was dependent upon Serbia for the materiel that you have listed there; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: After the break-up, the Igman facility found itself on territory occupied by the forces of the ABiH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I take it, sir, that from that point on, it was no longer supplied by Serbia for those materiels; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. So -- and that would apply, sir, would it not, to each of these facilities which found themselves outside of territory control by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I suppose it is so, unless they managed to procure materiel through brokers. For example, a broker could go to Serbia and purchase such materiel destined --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Buy such materiel and then sell it to a factory, say, in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That deals with that document; it can be taken off the screen. I'm sorry, just before it disappears ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: You mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, it can be removed from the screen, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: General, I'd like to move now to your report. And I will spend most of this afternoon and maybe some of tomorrow dealing with various matters that you have raised in your report, so keep a copy of it handy; we will be referring to it a lot this morning. The first paragraph I'd like to look at is paragraph 4, please, where you set out the methodology that you have adopted in compiling this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That is found, Your Honours, on page 4 of the English and also page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested, sir, with the very first thing that you mentioned in support of your methodology which you applied, which is that you had had conversations with participants of events. There's no further reference to those conversations in that paragraph. Can you tell us, please, who you had these conversations with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: A number of officers of the former JNA worked in the VRS at the time of the conflict. They now reside in Serbia and are familiar with the events which took place at the time. Some of them participated in logistics, and I believed it wise to make use of those people who were within the logistical system of the VRS in order to consult with them about what perspired [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well the difficulty, you see, general, is that when you do that you have to identify the sources of your information and identify in your report when you have relied on any information that they may have supplied you. And there are no references such as those anywhere in your report, are there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: There are no such references for the simple reason that I decided to use only credible documents as sources of information rather than making use of any information gained through conversations. I did not use a single piece of information for such conversations because I believe in such delicate matters we should base our research only on documents that are credible and available to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did conversations with -- or did these conversations result in notes being taken by you, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I gathered information from those conversations that I was interested in with a view to carrying out this analysis in order to compare them with the other information I had. I used that for my internal work as a control parameter to make sure that I have not made a mistake or omitted something in the course of drafting of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause, sir, and listen to my questions carefully. Did you keep notes of these conversations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I have no official notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did you record any of these conversations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Did you list anywhere the individuals that you have spoken to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: What did you do in situations where the information they provided to you conflicted with other information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I then double-checked everything, which means that I had to locate at least two published documents which would confirm the same figures. I never relied on a single oral piece of information to leave it as such and include it in the report. If there was a doubt anywhere, I went back and located a double source to confirm what I entered into the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Again, sir, the difficulty is we don't know when in your report you're required to do that. We can't tell from your report when you have discovered something that conflicts with other information you have been provided. How is a reader supposed to make that assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Conflicting information that we seem to be discussing now did exist at the time of the drafting of the document. Once such information found its way into the report, they were no longer conflicting because further corroboration was sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I repeat my question. Listen to my question. It is not clear from your report when that happened. It is not clear from your report when you were required to conduct further investigation because you had conflicting evidence. It is not clear from your report how you resolved that conflict. How is a reader supposed to make that assessment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I will cite an example which may clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No, pause. I'm not asking for examples, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, with regard to the question that you've posed, you've indicated that there's a failure of clarity in the report when that happened. His example may or may not be specific with regard to the assertion that has been made. And since the assertion that has been made contains multiple conclusions, the specific example the gentleman may be able to give may clarify your concern -- may clarify Mr. Thomas's concern. Because I don't want to get involved in a discussion that goes back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness can answer the question as put. And then if he wants to elaborate, he can also do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So, General, how is a reader supposed to draw their own conclusions as to whether how you resolved the conflict in evidence was the correct way to resolve it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that -- that's a -- first of all, it's a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It is. I can phrase the question in exact terms again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you would try to ask one question at a time, it would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: My question, General, was this: It is not clear from your report when that happened. It is not clear from your report when you were required to conduct further investigation because you had conflicting evidence. It's not clear from your report how you resolved that conflict. How is a reader supposed to make that assessment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Dear sir, item 4 is the answer to that question. And I'm trying to answer it orally again. Any potential conflicting information could only have existed at the stage of gathering available information which would be 4(a). As of the point in time when I carried out the selection of data with the highest degree of credibility, there was no conflict. The data contained in the report presented to the reader present no dilemma or no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, General, that's because, with all due respect, you present it in such a way as to make it seem that there is no conflict. So do I understand that effectively you're asking us to take --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly don't object to a vigorous cross-examination but I do object to an argumentative one. And there is an argument contained in Mr. Thomas's last question, which is with regard to "as to make it seem there is no conflict." Now, that particular language assumes that there is a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can ask the question a different way, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question which I need to ask in order to follow what you two are talking about. General, item (a) of paragraph 4, you tell us that the data you collected included conversations with participants and events. At page 51 starting from line 1 of today's transcript, you are recorded as saying the following: "There are no such references for the simple reason that I decided to use only credible documents as sources of information rather than making use of any information gained through conversations. I did not use a single piece of information for such conversations because I believe in such delicate matters we should base our research only on documents that are credible and available to all." Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if that is your answer, then it conflicts with item (a) of paragraph 4. In other words, you are saying now, today, that you didn't rely on conversations with participants, you relied only on documents that are credible and available to all. Now, therefore, conversations with participants -- now I'm putting it to you and I want you to say I'm wrong if you say so: Conversations with participants could not have been part of your methodology if we follow what you are saying today; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the document before you, there isn't a single piece of information that comes from any conversation with the participants of those events. They were eliminated in the preliminary phase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... therefore, am I therefore right to say that conversations with participants never formed part of your methodology? Because, in fact, you are telling me now that in this document there isn't a single conversation with any participant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, may I clarify my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I -- I just want you to confirm that I'm asking you: Am I correct in my interpretation? And if I'm not, just tell me, No, you are wrong. Then you can -- I'll ask you how, Am I wrong? Then you'll explain. Am I wrong to say conversations with participants did not form part of your methodology; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are partially wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, explain to me how wrong am I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such conversations were part of the methodology, but not a single piece of information obtained in such conversations was used in the course of the analysis. That is why there isn't a single reference to any of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that having had those conversations when you final drafted your report, you discarded all the information that you got from conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which means then that this report, it does not comprise any conversations, even though you may have used conversations when you collected your data; the data from conversations does not form part of this report. So the methodology for drafting this report excludes conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Completely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then paragraph (a) of 4 is not absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Following the questions of Judge Moloto, I have another question. During the course of your research, did you rely only on public documents or, as you said here, military and state documentations, report by international institution, books, newspaper articles, and special reports, legal regulation, et cetera. Then you mention (b), selection of data, expert evaluations, verification of expert assessments, and conclusions. My question is: Have you ever come during your research into secret type of documents? Were you privy to those secrets during your functions of the General Staff? First, did you come during the course of your research into secret documents, documents of secret nature? Yes or no, or I don't know; these are the three options.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly I came across such secret documents, but those documents were officially forwarded to the Defence team by the army, i.e., its office for the co-operation with the Defence team. There isn't a single document that I used that had not been obtained by the Defence through legal channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: If I understand well your answer, you had not been privy to any document because of your functions, documents of secret nature, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, perhaps -- I'm confused, and I think that's because you're asking questions on two equally interesting lines of inquiry, and I'm not sure which line of inquiry we're on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: The witness has replied that all of the documents of secret nature were obtained by the Defence, you know, have been sent to you. Out of that answer comes another question: In the nature of your functions during the time you had in your curriculum said you were from 2000 to 2004 director one technical officer, did you come ever in your functions through state secret documents related specifically to the help given by the Army of Yugoslavia either to Republika Srpska or to the Republic of Serbian Krajina? There are three possibilities: Yes, no, or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the course of my career I did come across such documents. But at the moment when I retired, I was duty-bound to return to the military all such documents that were put on the list. I was not allowed to keep a single such document in my possession after retirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: These documents were used in your report, those documents that you had been aware of even though you had returned later on to -- when you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are documents that I obtained from the archives of the Army of Yugoslavia by way of regular channels, by asking the Defence team to request such documents from the archive of the Army of Yugoslavia. I think that I made a request for two documents to be provided to me in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: An additional question: When you report on the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council - and I'll give you an example: Session number 21st of the Supreme Defence Council, at page -- decision of 7 June 1994, which is, I believe, in page 78, you discuss the 21st Session, 7 June 1994. And in paragraph 2.2, you said: "An explanation of the report on current problems in relations between the Yugoslav Army, the Army of Republika Srpska, and the Army of the Serbian Krajina was given by Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic." You said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: This conclusions or this summary represent exactly what has been said by Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic at that time in that session according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I copied this from the transcript from the minutes of that session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Do you exclude the possibility that there were other transcripts of that session that were of secret nature and that you had not access to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know anything about it. All I know is that I received the first transcripts with some pages darkened, so I couldn't see what was written on them. This is why I asked the Defence team to provide me the transcripts without any parts of them being redacted. I don't know who and why darkened certain pages of the transcript initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... are you aware that the help given to the Republika Srpska and to the Republic of Serbian Krajina in words of former President Milosevic were a state secret and as such were not disclosed? Were you aware of that or not? Or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, your -- the beginning of your question was missed apparently, and just so we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Yes. I am saying that are you aware, are you cognizant, were you cognizant that in your experience, or as an expert, the state secrets cover all help given by the Yugoslav Army to the Republika Srpska and to the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Were you aware of that or not? Or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know about that being a state secret comes from the transcripts that I saw, because at one of the sessions, when discussing these issues, they said this has to remain a state secret. I'm not sure exactly at which session it was said, but it was during one of those sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas. I'm sorry we interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: General, just going back to paragraph 4 again - we needn't have it on the screen - His Honour Judge Moloto had listed the various items; included amongst the collection of data was, for example, newspaper articles. Are you suggesting now, sir, that you did or did not use newspaper articles as a basis for your report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In my report I refer to several newspaper articles from the US press. There is not a single article used from the press from the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And can you assist us in how you determined that US press articles were reliable enough to support your investigations or conclusions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In the reports of the international community, they frequently make reference to the New York Times articles. And I used the articles referred to by the international community reports, SIPRI institute and so on. I only used the articles referred to in their reports and work. I would go back to check those articles. Also, in a book I saw that they said that the CIA had warned early on about the possible outcomes of the crises in Yugoslavia, so I tried to find that article to see what that CIA information initially looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just pause. All right. I'm sorry. I interrupted you prematurely. Sir, that is an example of telling us, the reader, how it was that you came to place certain reliance upon certain sources above others. My question to you, sir, is why the answer you have just given doesn't appear in your report? Why have you not shown us in your report why you accept some articles and not others, why you accept some hearsay information and not others?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph (b) of item 4 answers your question, Mr. Thomas. It says: "Selection of data with the highest degree of credibility." Whatever I considered to be of low level of credibility was not taken into account in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, I can see that, General. My point is this: We don't know how you assessed that. We don't know you, sir. You are asking us to accept your triage and evaluation of the documents as being reliable based on credibility, but you have given us no means to assess how you have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I find that Mr. Thomas's question is perhaps more suitable for a closing argument than it is for a factual examination of a witness. He has a matter of fact told us that he -- this witness has told us repeatedly that he has used objective data. If Mr. Thomas is suggesting that the testimony this witness has give within regard to such data as the data from CREST, the data from SIPRI, the data from other international organisations which is contained in his report is not credible, then he can ask him those kinds of questions; but that doesn't affect whether or not he himself is credible, it affects the issue of whether or not the data upon which he relied was credible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, that is exactly my point. Is how do we know how he assessed the credibility of the data. And what I'm asking him to provide is an explanation as to why the methodology for that assessment of credibility does not appear in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So, General, my question is, as I've just said to His Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us an explanation as to why the methodology for your assessment of credibility of individual sources does not appear in your report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: There are several aspects explaining why is that so. The first aspects is that what was published in the media of the warring sides --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just pause, sir --

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: -- is something that I considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause, sir. I'm not asking you to give us your methodology now. I'm asking you to explain why your methodology does not appear in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, we're shifting -- we're shifting the question and, I understand, in an attempt to cast doubt upon the credibility of the report itself. However, the question now asked, which is why your methodology does not appear in your report, is not accurate. That is a misstatement of the facts. Whether or not it is to his liking or to anyone else's liking, there is a very clear indication of the methodology which is used by this particular gentleman in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, the question I was permitted to put to General Djokic following Your Honours' ruling on the last objection was to ask him for an explanation as to why the methodology -- not for his report, but why the methodology for his assessment of credibility of individual sources doesn't appear in his report. And that's -- that's what I'm asking him. Why does that methodology not appear in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought that was the question you asked. You may put the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, General, do you understand the question? Can you give us an answer. Why does your methodology as to your assessment of credibility of individual sources not appear in your report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: See, this methodology of assessing the reliability of data used in this report has a theoretical aspect and a practical aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Pause, sir. Sir, I'm not asking you to give us now your methodology. I'm asking you to explain why you haven't put it in the report.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Because it is too broad of an issue to be explained here, and it is well known how such things are done. For example, you can reject the highest and the lowest data and only use the data from the middle section. This is one methodology of ensuring that you're using reliable data. There are other methodologies too that I can explain. But for the this particular expert report, and we wanted it to be of reasonable volume, I didn't think it necessary to include that piece of information into my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, so we have a report that runs, at least in the English version, to 130 pages, and your methodology is contained in paragraph 4. And perhaps, by specific extension, to paragraph 5 as well. Is that a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 I explain the methodology used, but I do not describe it in detail because I believed that not to be necessary. It is a theoretical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's look, for example, at paragraph 142.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Which is at page 50 in the English and 48, I think, Your Honours, in the B/C/S. I'm sorry, I'm a long way from the microphone. Page 50 in the English and page 48 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 142, sir, you are discussing the expert estimate, which is the bold entry we see in the chart above. We see that in the English version on the screen. I see you have it above -- in front of you in hard copy. And in paragraph 142 you are explaining how you've reached this expert's estimate. And beginning at line 4, you say: "To obtain this data, the author of this report made use of dozens of sources, estimates by other experts, estimates by international institutions which were present in Yugoslavia, newspaper articles, books, and his own data recorded at the time of the conflict." Now, sir, you use that expert estimate as a basis for a number of graphs and conclusions that you then present throughout your report. And my question, sir, is how can we evaluate those sources? You haven't referred to them except in the very limited sense by referring to the CREST report, the information provided to you specifically for this purpose by the VJ, and SIPRI, whom you discounted effectively. How do we evaluate your assessment of these dozens of sources?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: In table T1 that we are discussing now, we have source -- we have data from two sources which are credible and which do not have a difference greater than 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just pause, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The data that I obtained as an expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause, sir. We know about the two sources that you spoke of this morning. You don't in paragraph 142 or anywhere else in your report assist us to determine for ourselves whether the two sources you chose out of the dozens of sources you reviewed are actually the two most reliable. There's no explanation of how you reached that conclusion in your report, is there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: That is not true because when explaining how the CREST data was used, I say, I give reasons why I believe that data to be credible and why it was used. And since you asked me how are you supposed to verify whether the expert data is accurate, let me put a question back to you. Let me give you an explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I think we can agree on this, sir: Is it fair to say that you conducted your own assessment, you reached your conclusion as to what information you thought was the most reliable, and that is the information that you have presented in your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, however, the data I presented are in accordance with the data that have the highest level of credibility. Your Honour, may I answer the previous question of the Prosecutor concerning the reliability of the data in table T1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may do so, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two sources here, and I explained why these sources are credible. My data is somewhere in between these two credible sources which do not differ more than 10 per cent. Even if I had made a mistake, that mistake is not greater than 10 per cent. Every assessment necessarily involves a possibility of an error. Here we explain that that error cannot be greater than 10 per cent because the data from these two sources are significantly less than 10 per cent. The difference is 0.6 per cent, 2.2 per cent, et cetera. So, yes, there is a possibility that there's a mistake here, but not a large one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me see if I can try and help you. I think that there is a miscommunication between you and the Prosecutor, sir. What the Prosecutor is trying to find out from you is that on table T1 you use those two estimates of CREST and SIPRI, or CREST and somebody; however, in paragraph 142 you mention a whole lot of other sources which are not tabulated in T1. You, in writing the report, looked at all those sources and you decided you are discarding those sources, the dozens of sources that you are talking about, estimates by other experts, estimates by other international institutions which were present in Yugoslavia, newspaper articles, books, okay. You've discarded all those. And he says you are not explaining in your report on what basis you discarded those except for -- you say -- you're not explaining how you determined that they should be discarded. That's his problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have understood it. I can explain that detail and then that will hopefully correct the misunderstanding. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the methodology of looking for relevant values which was used here, one always discards the highest and the lowest values. And then for the remaining ones, one looks for middle values. And then you compare that to other data. This is the most acceptable methodology used when one is trying to make assessments. I, here, discarded all of the data that was outside of the limits defined by CREST and the JNA, the divergent data which was normal to discard, because nobody using the data in their literature could verify that. This is why I discarded the divergent data, and I only used the middle-level values in order to reach my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. You may continue, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, in answering a question a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And this, Your Honours, is at page 66, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: -- you said: "Every assessment necessarily involves a possibility of an error. Here we explain that that error cannot be greater than 10 per cent ..." and so on. My question, sir, is: Who is "we"? You say "here we explain," in the context of talking about your report. Who is "we," sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember using that term we. Maybe that's how it was interpreted. But if you want to repeat the entire sentence to me so that it is within the context, then I could perhaps answer your question. If I can have the exact interpretation of what you are referring to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's a perfectly fair request, sir. What you said was: "Here we explain that that error cannot be greater than 10 per cent because the data from these two sources are significantly less than 10 per cent."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Thomas and I both know that in common English usage plurals and singulars are often times interchanged. I don't know if the same is the case in the Serbian language, and I don't know whether -- and I don't want to go further with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed don't go further. Let the witness answer for himself. Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But my question was going to be whether we perhaps should get some assistance from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the witness will tell us if that assistance is necessary, Mr. Guy-Smith. Let the witness answer. Have you finished your question, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I have, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Mr. Djokic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours, in the context we are discussing now, if I said "we are explaining," then the following persons are participating in this discussion: Myself, the Prosecutor putting the question, and you, yourself, as the mediator; these are the three parties participating in the discussion about the methodology. If I said "we," then I meant us involved in giving this explanation. If I have to narrow it down, then I will tell you that I'm the one giving an explanation about the work that I have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: General, did anyone assist you in the analysis for and preparation of your written report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I did everything absolutely alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Now, did you provide your report for anyone to review or to anyone to review before it was filed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Only the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. General, if we go to paragraph 154 --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Which I think is on page 54 of the B/C/S, Your Honours, and 56 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: -- you reach a conclusion as to sources, or how weapons were redistributed following the JNA withdrawal. And if you look under (e), sir, we have "traded among the warring parties (to a lesser extent)." Now, during your testimony, sir, you referred to one occasion where the VRS provided artillery pieces and artillery ammunition to the Army of Croatia in exchange for fuel, but I understood that to be during the conflict or post-JNA withdrawal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: From the document of the VRS which I saw and as far as I recall, that trade between the warring parties took place after the withdrawal --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause. I'm sorry. Are you talking about the trade for oil?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Trade of oil and artillery ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. I owe you an apology. I interrupted you prematurely. So, do you confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But your question required a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It could have been a yes or a no answer. Exactly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do I understand, General, that the answer is yes, that happened after the JNA withdrawal? Sir, I'm sorry, did the trade of artillery for fuel occur after the JNA withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 154(e), you have no citation to any authority supporting your conclusion in subparagraph (e). Now, my question, sir, is do you have a citation anywhere in your report as support for that proposition?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I didn't specify that in the report, but there is such -- there are such documents in existence and they could be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause, sir. You need to listen to my question and answer only my questions. That was another yes/no question. Is it cited in the report; no. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 162, please, which is at page 61 of the English and expertly found in the B/C/S. I'm looking, Mr. Registrar, for subparagraph (e).

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Paragraph (e), sir, you state -- you draw a conclusion as to how the the VRS was able to equip forces numbering about 200.000 soldiers. And, again, the starting point that you took as to manpower and how it was equipped forms a key element in your analysis as to the overall assistance that was provided subsequently. You'll see, sir, that you say: "According to the estimates of the majority of military analysts ..." Now, I think you can see the difficulty with that comment, sir. Do you list anywhere those analysts?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I do but not in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you provide anywhere in your report variations on their assessment of the initial asymmetry that you discuss?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: I directly conveyed the positions of the analysts which took participation in the discussion at the American Institute for Peace whereby they proposed measures on how to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Just pause, sir, and listen to my question. Is that articulated in your report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: With their differences?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The differences in what?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, you refer, sir, to estimates, first of all. You refer to a findings of a majority of the military analysts. There exists in that one sentence a large margin of error on its face. So where do you provide any reference that assists us in evaluating your conclusion based on that sentence with a large margin of error?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Dear sir, in this report of mine, there is a chapter entitled "The Balance of Forces." In that chapter, it is specifically stated that all analysts claimed that there was an imbalance of forces. They agreed on that, but they did not take the same approach to how that imbalance should be addressed. I'm merely conveying what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. General, you can accept, I think, that those military analysts aren't named nor their estimates given?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: If you will bear with me, I will locate that for you. All right. I've found it. It is Article 217. Paragraph 217.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, that is one source; I agree. Where are the estimates of the rest of the military analysts?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: If one looks at that paragraph in detail, one realises that the discussion was organised by the United States Institute of Peace in which several people participated, different positions were presented, and for that purpose one would need to read the whole report of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. So the reference that you have in subparagraph (e) is a reference to this one report that is footnote 72; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: The footnote 72 is related to paragraph 217 so as to avoid any confusion about what is included. Paragraph 217 confirms what I stated in -- under (f).

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just trying to be clear. You refer in subparagraph (e) to the estimates of the majority of military analysts. When you say that, are you referring to this one report that is footnoted as footnote 72? Are these the majority of military analysts that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: At the meeting mentioned in footnote 72, it wasn't only the author who participated. There was a great number of military analysts --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just pause, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: -- present there who put forth their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, just pause. Listen to my question. The majority of military analysts, that term that you use, are you referring to those associated with this one report that is in footnote 72?

utterances.speaker: IVAN DJOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It would, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not done with you, Mr. Djokic; unfortunately you'll have to come back tomorrow. I must just warn you that now that you have taken the witness-stand, you may not discuss the case with anybody, least of all the Defence, until you are excused from further testimony. Can somebody tell me, are we sitting in the morning tomorrow or in the afternoon? In the morning I'm told. So we'll come back at 9.00 tomorrow morning in the same court. Okay. Court adjourned.
